facts.fact: The Puranas call the Satavahana rulers the 'Andhras'.
Another Puranic label for the dynasty is 'Andhra-bhrityas' ('Andhra servants').
The western Satavahana capital was Pratishthana (Paithan) on the Godavari.
The eastern Satavahana centre was Dhanyakataka, next to Amaravati on the Krishna.
Dharanikota was the fortified township attached to Dhanyakataka.
Satavahana rule lasted c. 2nd century BCE to the 3rd century CE.
The Krishna–Godavari delta exported cotton and muslin textiles to Rome.
Hala compiled the Gatha Saptasati in Maharashtri Prakrit.
Gunadhya wrote the Brihatkatha in Paisachi Prakrit at the Satavahana court.
The Gudimallam lingam (Chittoor) is among the earliest anthropomorphic Siva-lingas, of Satavahana-era art.
Simuka founded the Satavahana dynasty.
Coins of Simuka found at Kotilingala (Telangana) support the Telugu-region origin view.
The original home of the Satavahanas is debated between the Andhra (Telugu) country and the western Deccan (Maharashtra).
Satakarni I took the title Dakshinapathapati (Lord of Dakshinapatha); his queen Naganika issued the Naneghat inscription.
Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated the Saka ruler Nahapana.
The Nasik Prashasti praising Gautamiputra was issued by his mother Gautami Balashri.
Inscriptions of Vasishthiputra Pulumavi are found at Amaravati.
Yajna Sri Satakarni, the last great Satavahana, issued ship-type coins.
Yajna Sri Satakarni has an inscription at Chinna Ganjam in Prakasam district.
Satavahana coins were mostly of lead.
Satavahana records are in Prakrit written in the Brahmi script.
Ghantasala (Krishna district) was a port of foreign trade (with Kadura and Chaul, UPSC 2020).
Masulipatnam is the Maisolos/Maisolia of the Periplus and Ptolemy.
Amaravati lies in Palnadu district on the Krishna.
The Amaravati Mahachaitya was built in phases from c. 3rd century BCE to c. 250 CE.
The Amaravati Mahachaitya is protected by the ASI.
Andhra stupas carry five ayaka pillars on a platform on each of the four sides.
Amaravati is one of the three great early schools of sculpture with Gandhara and Mathura.
The Amaravati school worked in white-greenish limestone with crowded narrative reliefs.
The Gandhara school used grey schist (Greco-Roman look).
The Mathura school used red sandstone.
Amaravati art influenced Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.
The 'Amaravati Marbles' are in the Government Museum, Chennai and the British Museum.
Colin Mackenzie surveyed Amaravati in 1797–98.
Early Amaravati reliefs are aniconic — the Buddha shown by symbols such as the empty throne.
The Amaravati stupa mound was locally called Dipaladinne ('hill of lamps').
The Bhattiprolu relic caskets carry one of the earliest Brahmi specimens in South India.
The Bhattiprolu script is regarded as an ancestor of the Telugu-Kannada script.
The Bhattiprolu inscriptions name a king Kuberaka (Kubiraka).
Alexander Rea excavated the Bhattiprolu stupa in 1892.
Salihundam lies in Srikakulam district on the Vamsadhara.
Salihundam shows Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana phases.
Guntupalli has one of the earliest rock-cut chaityas in Andhra.
Thotlakonda and Bavikonda are hill-top monasteries near Visakhapatnam.
Jaggayyapeta stupa is famed for the 'Chakravartin/Mandhata' relief.
Ramatirtham (Vizianagaram) has Buddhist and Jain remains.
Sankaram near Anakapalli is also called Bojjannakonda.
Chandavaram (Prakasam) has a large double-terraced stupa.
Andhra Buddhist sites span the Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana phases.
The Andhra Ikshvakus ruled from Vijayapuri in the Nagarjunakonda valley.
The Ikshvakus succeeded the Satavahanas in the eastern Krishna valley.
The Andhra Ikshvakus ruled c. 225–340 CE.
The Andhra Ikshvakus are distinct from the legendary Ikshvakus of Kosala.
Vasishthiputra Chamtamula (Santamula I) founded the Andhra Ikshvaku dynasty.
Ikshvaku order: Chamtamula → Virapurushadatta → Ehuvala Chamtamula → Rudrapurushadatta.
The Ikshvakus kept the Satavahana habit of matronymic names (e.g. Vasishthiputra).
The Ikshvaku kings performed Vedic sacrifices while royal women patronised Buddhism.
Chamtisiri (Shantisri) endowed the Nagarjunakonda Mahachaitya.
The Ikshvakus began as Satavahana feudatories holding the title Mahatalavara.
The Matsya Purana's 'Shriparvatiya Andhras' are identified with the Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri.
The Ikshvaku kings were Shaivites.
Chamtamula is known from the Rentala and Kesanapalli inscriptions; his ashvamedha left coins and a kurma-chiti altar.
Buddhism flourished most under Virapurushadatta.
Virapurushadatta married Rudradhara-bhattarika, a princess of Ujjain (Western Kshatrapas).
The Ikshvaku kingdom reached its zenith under Ehuvala Chamtamula.
Ehuvala Chamtamula's Patagandigudem plates are the oldest known copper-plate charter in India.
Rudrapurushadatta is known from the Gurazala inscription.
The Ikshvakus were ended by the Pallavas (with the Abhiras occupying Vijayapuri).
Nagarjunakonda is named after Acharya Nagarjuna.
Nagarjunakonda had a rare stadium/amphitheatre besides mahachaityas and viharas.
Nagarjunakonda had a monastery for monks from Sri Lanka.
The Nagarjuna Sagar dam reservoir submerged the Nagarjunakonda valley.
The Nagarjunakonda relics were re-erected on a hilltop that is now an island museum.
Nagarjunakonda was discovered by A. R. Saraswati (1926) and excavated by A. H. Longhurst (1927–31).
R. Subrahmanyam led the 1954–60 rescue excavation of Nagarjunakonda.
Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika school.
Nagarjuna's doctrine is Sunyavada ('emptiness').
Nagarjuna wrote the Mula-madhyamaka-karika.
Tradition links Nagarjuna to Sriparvata (Nagarjunakonda–Srisailam hills).
Yogachara (Vijnanavada) is the school of Asanga and Vasubandhu, not Nagarjuna.
Nagarjuna's Suhrllekha ('Letter to a Friend') was addressed to a Satavahana king.
The Buddha is traditionally said to have preached the Kalachakra at Dhanyakataka.
The Mahasanghika-derived Chaitika (Andhaka) schools were strong in the Krishna valley.
The cult of Avalokitesvara is believed to have begun in Andhra.
Buddhism in Andhra declined from about the 6th century CE.
The Salankayanas (c. 300–440 CE) ruled from Vengi.
Vengi is identified with Pedavegi near Eluru.
The Salankayanas held the Godavari–Krishna doab.
The Salankayana emblem was the bull (Nandi), the source of their name.
The Salankayanas rose as feudatories of the Pallavas of Kanchi.
Hastivarman of Vengi (Salankayana) is named in Samudragupta's Allahabad Pillar inscription.
The Salankayanas worshipped Chitrarathasvami, the Sun god at Vengi.
Salankayana copper plates moved from Prakrit to Sanskrit.
The Brihatphalayanas (Kudura) and Ananda Gotrikas (Kandarapura) were minor contemporaries.
The Vishnukundins ruled in the 5th–7th centuries CE (c. 420–624).
The Vishnukundins took coastal Andhra from the Salankayanas.
Madhava Varma was the greatest Vishnukundin king and performed the ashvamedha.
Denduluru was a Vishnukundin capital.
Vishnukundin capitals included Indrapalanagara, Amarapura (Amaravati) and Bezwada.
Madhava Varma II married a Vakataka princess.
Madhava Varma IV bore the title Janashraya.
Manchana Bhattaraka, the last Vishnukundin, was expelled by the Chalukyas.
The name Vishnukundin is traditionally derived from Vinukonda.
The Vishnukundin family deity was Sriparvatasvami (Srisailam).
The Undavalli and Mogalrajapuram cave temples belong to the Vishnukundi period.
Bhairavakonda cave temples are also placed in the Vishnukundi period.
Pulakeshin II ended Vishnukundin rule and installed Kubja Vishnuvardhana.
The political centre shifted Dhanyakataka → Vijayapuri → Vengi.
The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi were founded in 624 CE by Kubja Vishnuvardhana.
Nannaya began the Telugu Mahabharatam under Rajaraja Narendra.
Under Kulottunga I the Vengi Chalukya and Chola thrones were united.
The Eastern Chalukyas ruled 624–1075 CE.
The Mayidavolu plates of Sivaskandavarman (Guntur) are an early Pallava Prakrit charter.
The Renati Cholas ruled Renadu (Kadapa region), 6th–8th century CE.
The Kalamalla inscription (c. 575 CE) of Erikal Mutturaju Dhananjaya is the earliest Telugu inscription.
The Renati Cholas were the first to use Telugu in royal records.
